overview: This file documents three aspects of Japan’s industrial capacity and recovery during the Allied occupation. An October 1946 memorandum estimates Japan’s surviving machine-tool inventory, productive capacity, and equipment potentially available for reparations; a May 1949 Army telegram supplies production and consumption statistics for copper, lead, zinc, and aluminum; and an August 1949 despatch and its enclosures investigate the wartime manufacture and possible postwar revival of tetraethyl lead. The latter correspondence records bombing damage, conversion of chemical plants to dyestuff production, the disposition of specialized equipment, patent concerns raised on behalf of a British company, and a detailed Japanese description of the manufacturing process.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Japanese machine-tool industry and inventories
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s surviving machine-tool inventory, productive capacity, and the number of tools and plants potentially available for reparations.
subfiles.summary: Memo estimates Japan's 1944 machine-tool stock at 788,700 units, postwar at 600,000, with capacity cut from 67,000 to 27,000 under the Interim Program, freeing about 200,000 tools for reparations.

subfiles.title: Army telegram reporting Japanese nonferrous-metal statistics
subfiles.about: Reports actual 1948 and estimated 1949 production and consumption figures for copper, lead, zinc, and aluminum in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Army telegram gives 1948 actual and 1949 estimated Japanese metric-ton figures for mined, refined, and consumed copper, lead, zinc, and aluminum, noting 1948 consumption reflects allocation-ticket shipments.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 532 transmitting correspondence on tetraethyl lead
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits three memoranda concerning Japan’s wartime and prospective postwar manufacture of tetraethyl lead.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser forwards an Australian inquiry, SCAP’s response, and a Nippon Soda memorandum describing the manufacturing process. The covering despatch suggests that this information about a lesser-known Japanese industry may interest several United States government agencies. Copies were also directed to the American embassies in Canberra and London.

subfiles.title: Australian Mission inquiry about resuming tetraethyl-lead manufacture
subfiles.from: Patrick Shaw, Head of the Australian Mission in Japan
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, attention G-2 Foreign Liaison
subfiles.about: Requests information about possible renewed Japanese manufacture of tetraethyl lead and associated intermediates, with particular concern for foreign patent rights.
subfiles.summary: Shaw, for Australia and Associated Ethyl, asks whether Japan might resume tetraethyl-lead manufacture at bomb-damaged prewar plants, seeking assurance foreign patents would be respected.

subfiles.title: SCAP report on Japanese tetraethyl-lead plants and patents
subfiles.from: Harry C. Kelly, Acting Chief, Scientific and Technical Division, Economic and Scientific Section, SCAP
subfiles.to: Head of the Australian Mission in Japan
subfiles.about: Identifies Japanese wartime tetraethyl-lead producers and explains the condition, conversion, or destruction of their plants and the status of relevant patents.
subfiles.summary: SCAP reports Nippon Soda, Hodagaya, naval fuel depots, and a near-ready Mitsui plant made tetraethyl lead; Nippon Soda and Mitsui converted to dyestuffs, none plan resumption, and discloses once-secret Navy patents Associated Ethyl might challenge.

subfiles.title: Nippon Soda description of the tetraethyl-lead manufacturing process
subfiles.about: Describes the successive chemical and mechanical operations used to manufacture tetraethyl lead and formulate ethyl fluid.
subfiles.summary: Nippon Soda details its tetraethyl-lead process (lead-sodium alloy and ethyl chloride reaction), waste-lead recovery, ethylene dibromide synthesis, and the ethyl fluid formula: 64.5% tetraethyl lead, 33.7% ethylene dibromide, plus minor additives.

interest: Shows postwar Japanese industrial demilitarization and tetraethyl-lead plant conversion, patents, machine tools, and nonferrous metals data.
